name: Matrices and Determinants
description: Matrix products, determinant properties, row operations and the link between determinants and invertibility.

questions.question: A is a 3×2 matrix and B is a 2×4 matrix. What are the dimensions of the product AB?
questions.explain: The inner dimensions must match (2 = 2) and the result takes the outer ones, giving 3×4. Note that BA is genuinely undefined here, since 4 does not match 3.

questions.question: If A is a 4×4 matrix with det(A) = 3, what is det(2A)?
questions.explain: Scaling a matrix scales every one of its n rows, so det(kA) = kⁿ·det(A) = 2⁴·3 = 48. Answering 6 treats the scalar as if it factored out only once, which is the most common error here.

questions.question: Two rows of a square matrix are swapped. What happens to its determinant?
questions.explain: A single row swap is an odd permutation, so it multiplies the determinant by −1. This is why row reduction has to track the number of swaps performed.

questions.question: A square matrix A is invertible if and only if:
options: All of its entries are non-zero
questions.explain: det(A) ≠ 0 is equivalent to full rank, independent rows and the existence of A⁻¹. A determinant of exactly 1 is a special case (unimodular), not a requirement.

questions.question: What is the determinant of an upper triangular matrix?
options: The sum of the diagonal entries
Always zero, since the lower half is zero
The product of all non-zero entries
The product of the diagonal entries
questions.explain: Cofactor expansion leaves only the diagonal product, which is why row reduction to triangular form is the practical way to compute determinants. The sum of the diagonal is the trace, a different quantity entirely.

questions.question: For square matrices A and B of the same size, which identity always holds?
options: det(AB) = det(BA) only when A is invertible
questions.explain: The determinant is multiplicative, so det(AB) = det(A)·det(B), and this also makes det(AB) = det(BA) hold unconditionally for square matrices. The determinant is not additive, so the first identity fails for almost any pair.

questions.question: Adding 5 times row 1 to row 3 of a matrix has what effect on its determinant?
questions.explain: Adding a multiple of one row to a different row does not change the determinant, which is what makes Gaussian elimination safe for computing it. Multiplying a single row by 5, by contrast, would multiply the determinant by 5.

questions.question: A 5×5 matrix has one row that is exactly twice another row. What is its determinant?
options: Twice the determinant of the matrix with that row removed
Undefined without knowing the other entries
questions.explain: Proportional rows are linearly dependent, so the matrix is singular and its determinant is 0. Equivalently, subtracting twice the first row leaves an all-zero row without changing the determinant.

questions.question: Which statement about matrix multiplication is correct?
options: It is commutative whenever both products are defined
It is commutative but not associative
It is neither associative nor commutative
It is associative but not generally commutative
questions.explain: (AB)C = A(BC) always holds, but AB and BA usually differ even when both are defined and square. This non-commutativity is why the order of transformations matters in graphics and in change-of-basis work.

questions.question: If A and B are invertible n×n matrices, what is (AB)⁻¹?
questions.explain: The order reverses: (AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹ = I. Writing A⁻¹B⁻¹ only works in the special case where A and B commute.
